title: backtracking, subsets, permutations, and combinations
concepts: Backtracking explores a decision tree by extending a partial candidate, recursively exploring it, and undoing the choice before trying another branch.
A state must contain exactly the information needed to resume a branch; mutable state must be restored on every return path or copied before recursion.
Subsets correspond to choose-or-skip decisions, permutations correspond to choosing an unused element at each position, and combinations impose an ordering rule to avoid duplicate orderings.
The search tree is often exponential or factorial because the output itself is large; complexity should count both explored states and the cost of constructing each output.
Sorting candidates can make duplicate values adjacent and support duplicate-skip rules, but the skip condition must preserve distinct valid choices at different recursion depths.
Pruning is sound only when a proven condition shows no completion of the current partial state can satisfy the goal.
A recursion depth bound, candidate index, or used-element structure prevents revisiting choices and makes the search invariant explicit.
Backtracking differs from dynamic programming when the goal is to enumerate solutions or when overlapping states do not allow safe aggregation into a reusable result.
